passage:
The rain had turned the bus into a steamy, packed box. Ishita, nine, held the rail with one hand and her little sister Tanuja’s wrist with the other. Mummy’s umbrella knocked a man’s elbow. “Sorry, that was my umbrella,” she said, and he nodded.
When the conductor held the bell so an old woman could climb down first, Mummy said, “Thank you, bhaiya.” Tanuja copied it in a loud little voice. A boy near the door pushed out without a word.
Later, Mummy waited her turn at the door, and as they got off, Ishita turned around. “Thank you,” she told the conductor. He looked surprised, then smiled.

qa.q: Why was Ishita holding Tanuja's wrist on the bus?
qa.a: The bus was packed, so Ishita kept hold of her little sister Tanuja's wrist while holding the rail with the other hand.

qa.q: What might Ishita have been thinking when she turned round to thank the conductor?
qa.a: Ishita probably felt a shy little pride and wanted to do what Mummy had done, since nobody told her to turn round and say thank you.

qa.q: What does Ishita's thank-you at the end suggest about what she learned on the bus?
qa.a: Nobody told Ishita to say it. She had watched Mummy apologise, wait and thank, and she did the same when she got the chance.

qa.q: How might the man whose elbow was bumped have felt about Mummy's apology?
qa.a: He may have felt his crowded discomfort ease a little, since a quick apology treated him as a person. He nodded, which suggests he accepted it.

grounding: Shows Mummy modelling thanks, patience and apology on a crowded bus, and a child copying without being told.

passage:
On Saturday, Elizabeth and her son Tanvir joined the long line at the vegetable weighing counter. Elizabeth waited without sighing while a man in front argued about a price. A woman’s bag swung and bumped Elizabeth’s arm. “Oh, sorry, I was in your way,” Elizabeth said, though it wasn’t her fault, and the woman laughed.
At the counter she said, “Thank you, that looks fresh,” and the young seller looked up and his tired face softened. Tanvir, eight, said nothing. He only watched.
On Monday at school, Tanvir bumped into a girl carrying books. “Sorry,” he said quickly, and bent to pick one up before anyone told him to.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth say to the seller at the counter?
qa.a: She said, “Thank you, that looks fresh.”

qa.q: What might the seller have been feeling when his face softened?
qa.a: The seller was probably feeling a little more appreciated after a long, tiring day. A simple thank-you from a customer in the line changed his mood.

qa.q: What choice did Tanvir make at school on Monday, and where might it have come from?
qa.a: He apologised at once and helped pick up the book without being told. He had seen Elizabeth do the same kind of thing at the market.

qa.q: How might the woman with the swinging bag have felt about Elizabeth's apology?
qa.a: She may have felt relieved that no one was angry, and even a little amused, since she laughed. Elizabeth's kindness turned a small bump into a friendly moment.

grounding: Shows Elizabeth's thanks, patient waiting and apology in a market line, and Tanvir later copying that manner at school.

passage:
'Two tickets to Charminar, please,' said Hafsa, handing over the coins. 'Thank you, bhaiya.'
The conductor blinked. 'Welcome, madam.'
Avni tugged her sleeve. 'Ammi, why do you always say thank you? It's his job.'
'Because he's been standing since six this morning,' Hafsa said. The bus lurched, and Hafsa's bag bumped a man in the next seat. 'Oh, sorry, uncle.'
'No problem, beti.'
At the stop, a crowd pushed toward the door. Hafsa held Avni's hand and waited. 'Let the grandmother go first.'
'But we'll be last!'
'We'll still get off.'
The next week, on the same bus, Avni handed the conductor her own coins. 'Thank you, bhaiya,' she said, and looked at her mother to see if she'd noticed.

qa.q: Where were Hafsa and Avni going?
qa.a: To Charminar.

qa.q: What does Avni looking at her mother after thanking the conductor suggest?
qa.a: Avni felt proud and hoped Ammi noticed she was copying her good manners.

qa.q: How did Hafsa teach manners without lecturing?
qa.a: By doing it herself: thanking the conductor, apologising for the bump and letting the grandmother go first, with short reasons when asked.

qa.q: How might the conductor feel when thanked?
qa.a: Surprised and a little pleased, since he has been standing since six and rarely hears it.

grounding: A mother teaches public manners by example on a bus, and her daughter copies her the next week.

passage: I used to lecture my daughter Rekha about manners, and it never stuck. Then one Saturday at the vegetable market, I realised she wasn't listening to my words at all; she was watching me. I'd snapped at the vendor about the price of tomatoes, and five minutes later Rekha snapped at her little cousin for taking her ball. Same tone. So I tried something. I started thanking the auto driver, waiting behind the old man at the cash machine without sighing, apologising when my bag bumped someone. I didn't point any of it out. Three weeks later, in the temple queue, Rekha stepped aside for a woman with a baby and said, 'You go first, aunty.' I'm Chetan, and that's the best lesson I never taught.

qa.q: What did Rekha say to the woman with a baby?
qa.a: 'You go first, aunty.'

qa.q: How did Chetan feel after hearing Rekha snap in the same tone?
qa.a: Chetan felt uncomfortable and a bit ashamed, realising Rekha was copying Chetan's behaviour, not the lectures.

qa.q: What changed in Chetan's way of teaching manners?
qa.a: Chetan stopped lecturing and started modelling: thanking the driver, waiting patiently and apologising, without pointing it out.

qa.q: How might the woman with the baby see Rekha?
qa.a: As a kind, thoughtful child, and she was likely grateful to be let ahead in the queue.

grounding: A parent realises children learn manners by watching, and changes their own public behaviour instead of lecturing.

passage: Class 4 trip note, museum visit, Friday. Zainab, a parent volunteer, came with us. At the ticket counter she thanked the guard by the name on his badge. When a school group from elsewhere pushed ahead, she simply waited and said to our children, 'They must be in a hurry; we'll still see everything.' In the café she apologised to a waiter when she knocked a spoon down. I noticed Ojas watching her closely. Later, at the dinosaur gallery, Ojas held the door for an elderly man and said, 'Please go first.' No one had told Ojas to. I will ask Zainab to volunteer again, and on Monday in class we will talk about what the children noticed on the trip.

qa.q: What did Ojas say to the elderly man?
qa.a: 'Please go first.'

qa.q: What might Ojas have been thinking while watching Zainab closely?
qa.a: Ojas seemed curious and impressed by how calmly and kindly Zainab behaved, and quietly decided to copy it.

qa.q: What does the teacher plan, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Asking Zainab to volunteer again and discussing on Monday what the children noticed, so they reflect on the example they saw.

qa.q: How might the guard feel being thanked by name?
qa.a: Surprised and respected, noticed as a person rather than part of the building.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child copying the calm public manners a parent volunteer modelled on a trip.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Went to the market with Papa on the city bus in Aizawl today. I noticed three things he did. Getting on, he said "Thank you, ma'am" to the conductor, Lalremsiami aunty, even though she only gave us tickets. At the vegetable stall a man pushed in front of us. Papa just waited. I was so annoyed! On the way back the bus lurched and Papa bumped an old lady's basket. He said sorry and picked up her oranges. She smiled and gave me one! Papa never told me to do any of this. But when we got off, I said thank you to the conductor too. She winked at me.
Ankita

qa.q: What did Papa say to the conductor when he got on?
qa.a: He said "Thank you, ma'am" to the conductor.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel when the man pushed in front?
qa.a: Ankita was annoyed, even though Papa stayed calm and simply waited.

qa.q: Why did Papa's way of teaching manners work?
qa.a: He never lectured; he thanked, waited and apologised himself, and Ankita copied the thank-you on the way out.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami aunty feel when passengers thank her?
qa.a: She probably feels noticed and pleased, which is why she winked at Ankita.

grounding: Ankita's diary shows a parent teaching public manners by example, thanking the conductor, waiting and apologising, and the child copying.
